guides.title: Set up Friendswood alerts on both phones
guides.scenario: One of you is in the garden while the other is out of town. A water notice sent to only one phone leaves half the household guessing.
steps: Before a storm, get both phones, your street address and the email each person checks. The instructions here work offline. Sending the registration takes internet access. If you need help getting signed up, call Friendswood Emergency Management at 281-996-3335 during office hours.

On the first phone, open the city’s Emergency Notifications page in References. Under Friendswood Alerts, tap Sign up for Alerts. The next page says City of Friendswood – TX Alerts and is hosted by Smart911. The City Newsletter is a separate subscription.

Choose your language and enter your name, email and user ID. Your email can be your user ID. Choose a password with at least eight characters, including uppercase, lowercase, a number and a symbol. Enter it again to confirm.

Enter the number of the phone in your hand and select Mobile. To receive texts, check Opt-In to Public Service SMS Alerts. Leave Group Code blank unless you were given one. Review the terms, check the agreement box and tap Create Account.

Complete the phone verification when prompted. For a text, enter the code from the message. For an automated call, follow its instructions. If nothing arrives, recheck the number before requesting another verification.

In your profile, add or confirm the home street address, including any unit number. Some city warnings go only to addresses inside the affected area. Check your saved address and delivery choices before signing out.

Repeat on the second phone with that person’s details. Each of you should be able to sign back in and see the correct number and home address. When the city next issues a test or notice, check both phones.

Check the phone’s separate wireless emergency alerts too. On a U.S. iPhone open Settings, then Notifications, and scroll to Government Alerts. Review Emergency Alerts and Public Safety Alerts. On Android, search Settings for “wireless emergency alerts.” These settings control broadcast warnings. Friendswood still needs your city registration for local calls and texts.
After a move or new phone number, use Modify or Unsubscribe on the same city page. If cell service fails, listen to local weather bulletins on a battery-powered NOAA radio (Houston, 162.400 MHz).
guides.overview: Enrollment details checked November 16, 2026. Use the city link for later changes. A city subscription lets Friendswood send local warnings by phone, text or email.
sources: National Weather Service · Texas transmitters and county codes

illustrations.step: On the first phone, open the city’s Emergency Notifications page in References. Under Friendswood Alerts, tap Sign up for Alerts. The next page says City of Friendswood – TX Alerts and is hosted by Smart911. The City Newsletter is a separate subscription.
illustrations.title: Register each person’s usual contact
illustrations.alt: A home address branches to two different phones. Each person has their own registration.
illustrations.caption: Check both registrations. A message on one person’s phone tells you only that their contact is reachable.

guides.title: Make a wallet card for meeting up
guides.scenario: The phones are at 3% and a blocked street keeps you from meeting at home.
steps: Choose one meeting point outside the home and a second outside the neighborhood. Use a specific entrance or landmark everyone can describe.
Ask a willing out-of-area contact to relay messages. Write their number and both meeting places on each card.
Agree what to text when separated. Try “Safe at the library, staying here, next check-in at 4.” Include the date if the incident spans several days.
Swap cards and describe both meeting places from memory. Correct ambiguous wording and return each card to its wallet.
guides.overview: The card answers three questions without a charged phone. Where should I go, who can relay a message, and when should I expect another update?

illustrations.step: Ask a willing out-of-area contact to relay messages. Write their number and both meeting places on each card.
illustrations.title: Name the entrance on both copies
illustrations.alt: A wallet card contains spaces for nearby and farther meeting places, the relay contact, and the next check-in.
illustrations.caption: Make both copies from the same wording. A named entrance gives each person something they can actually find.

guides.title: Pack the last ten minutes of an evacuation
guides.scenario: The bags are by the door. The everyday things you still need are on a charger, in the refrigerator and beside the bed.
steps: Walk from the bedroom to the exit on an ordinary day. Write down the items you use daily that cannot stay packed, including glasses, medication, keys and mobility aids.
Beside each item, write its usual location and who will collect it. Put the short list on the packed bag.
Place the open collection bag beside the exit. Practice collecting the items and check that one person can still open the door and manage a pet carrier.
If an order or immediate danger requires leaving now, go. The rehearsal helps you identify the essentials that should already be close at hand.
guides.overview: The last-minute list bridges the gap between a packed evacuation bag and a lived-in home. Update it when a routine or prescription changes.

illustrations.step: Beside each item, write its usual location and who will collect it. Put the short list on the packed bag.
illustrations.title: Give each loose item a home and a collector
illustrations.alt: A tag attached to a bag lists an example item, its location and the person collecting it.
illustrations.caption: Give the last-minute list a permanent place on the bag. Assign each loose item to someone who can reach it.

guides.title: Choose two reachable evacuation destinations
guides.scenario: The usual destination is across a flooded route or outside your host’s availability.
steps: Choose a primary and a backup destination outside the likely affected area. Call ahead about availability, accessibility and pets.
Write the addresses, contact numbers and access needs on paper. Identify alternate routes without assuming a mapped road will be open.

Give one person the host phone numbers and the other the paper map. Mark both destinations and a dry alternative before storm season. During an evacuation, get current orders from Friendswood Alerts or broadcast radio and follow local traffic control. A printed route cannot tell you which roads are open.
Practice locating both destinations without internet. If a route is covered in water or barricaded, turn around and seek an official alternative.
guides.overview: A destination becomes usable when a person can receive you and a safe route remains available. Keep the two contacts beside the household’s departure list.
sources: National Weather Service · During a flood

illustrations.step: Write the addresses, contact numbers and access needs on paper. Identify alternate routes without assuming a mapped road will be open.
illustrations.title: Trace a dry alternative
illustrations.alt: Trace a dry alternative. Start at the dot. The direct road reaches water at the cross. Check the entire alternate route with local authorities before leaving.
illustrations.caption: Start at the dot. The direct road reaches water at the cross. Check the entire alternate route with local authorities before leaving.

guides.title: Arrange evacuation with mobility or sensory needs
guides.scenario: An ordinary doorway, noisy shelter or high vehicle step can turn into the hardest part of leaving.
steps: Ask the person what help they want with transfers, directions and communication. Write their preferences in their words.
With permission, ask a primary helper and a backup how they can help. Confirm the vehicle can accommodate the person and equipment.

In Texas, call 2-1-1 before an emergency and ask for STEAR registration. Have the home address, callback number and specific transport or equipment needs ready. The registry helps local planners. Keep your own ride and backup arrangements because registration does not guarantee pickup.
Call the destination to verify step-free access, charging outlets, service-animal arrangements and any other specific need.
Walk the route to the vehicle together in daylight. Note any barrier and arrange qualified help with transfers that cannot be made safely.
guides.overview: A workable plan names the helper, transport and receiving location. Give the person a copy they can present directly to responders or shelter staff.
sources: Texas Division of Emergency Management · STEAR registration

illustrations.step: Walk the route to the vehicle together in daylight. Note any barrier and arrange qualified help with transfers that cannot be made safely.
illustrations.title: Rehearse the route together
illustrations.alt: Rehearse the route together. Follow the route from the door to the passenger side. Check each turn and threshold with the person using their usual aid.
illustrations.caption: Follow the route from the door to the passenger side. Check each turn and threshold with the person using their usual aid.

guides.title: Inventory the pantry by meals and water needed
guides.scenario: A shelf full of dry rice looks reassuring until the water is off and you cannot cook.
steps: Draw three columns for ready to eat, needs safe water, and needs heat. Sort a representative three-day selection for both of you.
Build actual breakfasts, lunches and dinners from the items. Write the servings on each line and include drinks and any dietary constraints.
Set aside one whole day of meals that can be eaten straight from the shelf. Check that the can opener works on the cans you chose.
Eat one trial meal on an ordinary day. Replace what you used and revise quantities based on what the two of you actually ate.
guides.overview: You finish with a menu you have tested and the water and cooking requirements for the other meals. A list of cans alone cannot show those dependencies.

illustrations.step: Draw three columns for ready to eat, needs safe water, and needs heat. Sort a representative three-day selection for both of you.
illustrations.title: Sort by what the meal needs
illustrations.alt: Sort by what the meal needs. Left to right, canned fruit can be eaten as packed, powdered milk needs safe water, and dry pasta needs water and heat.
illustrations.caption: Left to right, canned fruit can be eaten as packed, powdered milk needs safe water, and dry pasta needs water and heat.

guides.title: Size a drinking-water reserve for two people
guides.scenario: You have room for a few cases but want to know exactly how many days they buy.
steps: Allow at least one gallon per person per day for at least three days. For two people the starting amount is six gallons. Plan extra for heat, illness and pets.
Add the labeled volumes of the containers. Six one-gallon jugs or forty-eight 16-fluid-ounce bottles each supply six gallons.
Choose a cool location away from sunlight, chemicals and areas likely to flood. Store manageable containers where both people can lift them.

For water you fill yourself, wash a food-grade container with soap and rinse. To sanitize the empty container, mix one teaspoon of unscented household bleach (5–9% sodium hypochlorite) into one quart of water. Cap and shake to wet all inside surfaces. After at least 30 seconds, pour out the solution and let the container air-dry. This mixture is for cleaning the container.
Fill the dry container with safe drinking water, cap tightly and write the fill date on it. Replace home-filled water every six months. Follow the date on commercially bottled water.
guides.overview: Write the reserve in days as well as gallons. If guests arrive or conditions get hotter, that number immediately tells you what needs reconsidering.

illustrations.step: Allow at least one gallon per person per day for at least three days. For two people the starting amount is six gallons. Plan extra for heat, illness and pets.
illustrations.title: Count the days in rows
illustrations.alt: Six one-gallon jugs form three columns, with one row per person. Each column supplies both people for one day at the starting allowance.
illustrations.caption: Each pictured jug holds one gallon. One column represents a day for two people at the starting allowance in this guide.

guides.title: Run a bedroom-to-street fire drill
guides.scenario: It’s easy to name the front door at lunch. Can both of you find another way out from where you sleep?
steps: Sketch doors and windows and identify two exits from each room where possible. Clear obstructions and check that intended exits open.
Choose one recognizable meeting spot outside, away from the building and clear of firefighters’ access.
Walk the plan together after announcing the drill. Pretend the usual exit is blocked and name the alternate. Never climb or jump for practice.
At the meeting point count everyone. In a real fire, stay out, call 911 from safety and tell firefighters about anyone missing.
guides.overview: A drill reveals the sticking latch, blocked path or vague meeting place while there is time to fix it. Repeat after a furniture or sleeping-arrangement change.
sources: U.S. Fire Administration · Home fire escape plans

guides.title: Prepare a care card for medications and equipment
guides.scenario: Someone else has to speak to a pharmacy or equipment supplier while you are away from home.
steps: Copy current medicine names, strengths and prescribed schedules from the labels. List known allergies, pharmacy, prescriber and a contact who can clarify changes.
For each powered device, add make, model, supplier number and the location of its instructions and approved backup equipment.
Ask the pharmacist how any temperature-sensitive medicine should travel and what to do after a storage interruption. Record their product-specific answer.
Date the card, review it together and keep a private copy with the travel kit. Replace old copies when instructions change.
guides.overview: The care card gives a professional an accurate starting point for reconciliation. It also helps the partner who usually leaves refills and equipment calls to the other person.
sources: FDA · Home health and consumer devices

illustrations.step: Copy current medicine names, strengths and prescribed schedules from the labels. List known allergies, pharmacy, prescriber and a contact who can clarify changes.
illustrations.title: Read the identifying details from the container
illustrations.alt: An example container has arrows pointing to the product name and strength as printed, without example doses.
illustrations.caption: Use the wording printed on the actual container. A clear photo preserves the small print when someone else needs to read it.

guides.title: Measure the real reach of a battery backup
guides.scenario: The power bank says it is full. Nobody knows whether it charges the household’s actual phone and cable.
steps: Charge the power bank as instructed. Pick a phone at a known starting percentage and plug it in with the cable you plan to pack.
After a timed interval record the phone’s charge, the bank’s indicator and whether using the phone interrupted charging.
Pack the cable with the bank and label the last successful test. Store and recharge as directed by its maker.
Keep medical equipment on its own manufacturer-approved backup plan. Take a damaged, swollen or overheating battery out of use.
guides.overview: The test establishes that this cable, connector and battery work together. A nominal capacity printed on the case cannot establish that by itself.

illustrations.step: Pack the cable with the bank and label the last successful test. Store and recharge as directed by its maker.
illustrations.title: Bundle the cable with its power bank
illustrations.alt: A power bank and matching cable sit together in one pouch. Both connectors are visible.
illustrations.caption: Store the working cable beside the device. A date on the pouch records the last time you tested the pair.

guides.title: Make a plan for powered medical equipment
guides.scenario: A battery alarm during a blackout is the wrong time to discover a device’s backup limit.
steps: List the devices that must keep running and who supplies each one. Call the supplier or care team about approved backup power and safe transfer procedures.
Ask how to recognize remaining operating time, which alarms matter and at what point to leave for a powered location.
Confirm a destination that can support the equipment and arrange transport with a backup contact. Include travel time when choosing the departure threshold.
Keep the plan and supplier numbers with the device. If failure threatens breathing or another essential function, call 911 immediately.
guides.overview: A backup plan has a time to act, a destination and someone who can get you there. Do not disconnect essential equipment to estimate its runtime.
sources: FDA · Home health and consumer devices

illustrations.step: Ask how to recognize remaining operating time, which alarms matter and at what point to leave for a powered location.
illustrations.title: Read the battery indicator
illustrations.alt: Read the battery indicator. Inogen Rove 6 example. On battery power the display estimates remaining charge or running time. Ask the supplier how to plan for a low-battery alarm.
illustrations.caption: Inogen Rove 6 example. On battery power the display estimates remaining charge or running time. Ask the supplier how to plan for a low-battery alarm.

guides.title: Photograph what you own before the next storm
guides.scenario: If a room were empty tomorrow, listing everything in its drawers would be surprisingly hard.
steps: Stand at the doorway and photograph the room, then open storage areas and capture groups of items.
For major appliances, tools and electronics, take a second photo of the model and serial label and save any matching receipt.
Name the set by room and date. Store a protected copy somewhere accessible if the house and phone are both unavailable.
Have the other person retrieve one item by name. Fix the filing system now if it takes several guesses.
guides.overview: A wide photo establishes where an item belonged. The close-up establishes which item it was, making replacement and claim paperwork easier.

illustrations.step: For major appliances, tools and electronics, take a second photo of the model and serial label and save any matching receipt.
illustrations.title: Take a wide photo and a label photo
illustrations.alt: An appliance in a room is paired with a close photo of its model and serial label.
illustrations.caption: Keep the two images together. The room view places the item and the label identifies the particular model.

guides.title: Read a water notice before turning on the tap
guides.scenario: A city text mentions the water system. The word after “do not” changes what you can safely do.
steps: Read the complete notice, its affected area and its issue time. Preserve a copy while your phone has service.

For a Texas boil water notice, use bottled water or bring tap water to a vigorous rolling boil. Start timing once the whole surface keeps bubbling. Boil for two minutes, then cool in a clean, covered container. Follow any different instructions in the notice. Use safe water for drinking, brushing teeth, preparing food and making ice. Turn off the fridge dispenser and ice maker.

For a do-not-drink notice, use bottled water for ingestion and food preparation. Boiling will not remove hazardous chemicals. For a do-not-use notice, avoid all tap-water contact covered by the order.
Place a reminder at every used tap and tell both people. Keep the measures in place until the utility lifts the notice and gives its flushing or ice-disposal instructions.
guides.overview: Your household’s plan should reflect the exact notice, including what to do after it ends. The absence of odor or discoloration cannot tell you the water is safe.
sources: Texas Commission on Environmental Quality · Understanding boil water notices

illustrations.step: Read the complete notice, its affected area and its issue time. Preserve a copy while your phone has service.
illustrations.title: Read all three notice fields
illustrations.alt: Read all three notice fields. Example notices can say “Boil water,” “Do not drink,” or “Do not use.” Match the exact instruction, area and effective time.
illustrations.caption: Example notices can say “Boil water,” “Do not drink,” or “Do not use.” Match the exact instruction, area and effective time.

guides.title: Set up a handwashing station without a running tap
guides.scenario: The water is off and the same pair of hands has to handle the trash and prepare lunch.
steps: Stand the jug on a stable surface with its spout above the catch basin. Place soap and a clean drying supply on the clean side.
Wet hands with safe running water, lather all surfaces for at least 20 seconds, rinse from the spout and dry.
Keep used water out of the clean jug. Empty the catch basin according to local wastewater directions before it overflows.
Check soap, clean water and towels before the next meal. If soap and water are unavailable, use sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol where appropriate.
guides.overview: A one-way path from clean jug to hands to catch basin keeps multiple people from dipping into a shared bowl.
sources: CDC · Personal hygiene during an emergency

guides.title: Start a refrigerator outage clock
guides.scenario: You wake up to a dark kitchen and do not know exactly when the electricity failed.
steps: Record the last known time power was on and the first time you noticed the outage. Use the earlier time for planning if the start is uncertain.
Leave doors closed. An unopened refrigerator typically holds safe cold for about four hours. A closed full freezer lasts about 48 hours and a half-full one about 24.
If suitable ice and a cooler are already available, transfer perishables before their safe window ends and hold them at 40°F or below.

Without evidence the food stayed at 40°F or colder, discard refrigerated perishables after four hours without power. Examples include milk, eggs, meat, fish, leftovers, cooked rice, cut fruit and shredded cheese. If you know they were above 40°F for more than two hours, discard them sooner.
Intact blocks of hard cheddar or Parmesan, butter, whole uncut fruit and plain bread can generally be kept after a power outage if uncontaminated. Discard doubtful foods without tasting.
Frozen food with ice crystals still present or a measured temperature of 40°F or below can generally be refrozen or cooked. Discard thawed ice cream and frozen yogurt.
guides.overview: The door note preserves timing that is easy to forget during a long outage. Ice crystals or a measured temperature of 40°F or below help assess frozen items.
sources: FoodSafety.gov · Food safety during a power outage

illustrations.step: Record the last known time power was on and the first time you noticed the outage. Use the earlier time for planning if the start is uncertain.
illustrations.title: Record the uncertainty
illustrations.alt: Two marks on a timeline show when power was last known to be on and when it was first noticed off. The outage began somewhere in between.
illustrations.caption: Write the two actual clock times down. A later observation does not tell you exactly when the power failed.

guides.title: Turn back from a flooded route
guides.scenario: On the drive home, water covers the lane near an underpass. A truck ahead makes it through.
gear: Paper map or official route update
steps: Slow down on dry pavement and stop before the water. Leave space to turn safely.
Turn back without entering the water or passing a barricade. A larger vehicle’s crossing reveals little about the road beneath it.
Seek higher ground via a dry route. If none is available, remain in a safe location and check official information rather than following an unverified shortcut.
Update your contact from a safe stop. If trapped or in immediate danger, call 911 and give your location and landmarks.
guides.overview: Getting home later is a successful outcome here. Your next useful piece of information is a confirmed dry route, which may be different from the one shown on a saved map.
sources: National Weather Service · During a flood

illustrations.step: Turn back without entering the water or passing a barricade. A larger vehicle’s crossing reveals little about the road beneath it.
illustrations.title: Trace a dry alternative
illustrations.alt: Trace a dry alternative. Start at the dot. The direct road reaches water at the cross. Check the entire alternate route with local authorities before leaving.
illustrations.caption: Start at the dot. The direct road reaches water at the cross. Check the entire alternate route with local authorities before leaving.

guides.title: Send one useful storm check-in
guides.scenario: Calls drop and a family message thread fills with guesses about who is safe.
steps: From a safe location send one short update to the agreed contact. Include your name, time, location, condition and next check-in.
Use an unambiguous landmark. For example, “Cindy and Glenn, 3:20 pm, inside the north library entrance, both safe. Next text at 5.”
Ask the contact to relay it. Conserve the battery and avoid repeatedly calling everyone in the group.
If you need emergency aid, call 911 as soon as possible. A family text is not a request for dispatch.
guides.overview: A time and next contact window help the reader distinguish an old message from a new development when delivery is delayed.

illustrations.step: Use an unambiguous landmark. For example, “Cindy and Glenn, 3:20 pm, inside the north library entrance, both safe. Next text at 5.”
illustrations.title: Write one complete check-in
illustrations.alt: Write one complete check-in. Give a time, a recognizable location, current status and the next planned contact.
illustrations.caption: Give a time, a recognizable location, current status and the next planned contact.

guides.title: Hand off a pet to a temporary caretaker
guides.scenario: A pet-friendly friend can help, but has never fed the animal or managed its carrier.
steps: Write the pet’s name, identifying marks, feeding routine, veterinary contact, owner contact and any prescription instructions exactly as labeled.
Label the carrier and food and pack familiar restraint equipment. Include a current photo and a document showing the animal belongs with you.
Tell the caretaker how to prevent an escape during transfers. Arrange a quiet enclosed room for opening a cat carrier.
Agree how often to check in, who can authorize veterinary care and where you will reunite. Keep a copy of the handoff details.
guides.overview: A caretaker needs day-to-day instructions as well as a way to return the animal. Specific food and handling notes help a displaced pet keep familiar routines.

illustrations.step: Label the carrier and food and pack familiar restraint equipment. Include a current photo and a document showing the animal belongs with you.
illustrations.title: Match the carrier and care card
illustrations.alt: Match the carrier and care card. Put the same pet name on the carrier and supplies. Keep the contact and veterinarian details readable during handoff.
illustrations.caption: Put the same pet name on the carrier and supplies. Keep the contact and veterinarian details readable during handoff.

guides.title: Keep a paper log when shifts change
guides.scenario: One of you goes to sleep during a long outage. The other inherits half a dozen unfinished tasks.
steps: Draw four columns for time, observation, action and next check. Use local time and include the date at midnight.
Record facts separately from estimates. For example, record the refrigerator’s measured temperature separately from the estimated outage start.
Circle the next check for each active issue and assign a person. Cross out completed tasks with a single line so the history remains readable.
Read the open items aloud at handoff. Put critical care information in the person’s separate medical record.
guides.overview: The log tells the next person what changed and which decisions are still open. It also creates a timeline if the utility or insurer later asks for one.

illustrations.step: Draw four columns for time, observation, action and next check. Use local time and include the date at midnight.
illustrations.title: Fill in the next check
illustrations.alt: Fill in the next check. Example entry. The person taking over can see what changed, what was done and when to look again.
illustrations.caption: Example entry. The person taking over can see what changed, what was done and when to look again.

guides.title: Decide which room stays cool or when to leave
guides.scenario: The house is heating up and the power company has no restoration estimate.
steps: Check the indoor temperature and the people in the room. If someone is confused, collapses or shows signs of heat stroke, call 911 and start cooling immediately.
Contact an accessible air-conditioned destination and confirm it is open, reachable and suitable for everyone, including pets if needed.
While arranging transport, reduce sun through windows and postpone heat-producing tasks. Keep drinking water accessible to alert people who can swallow.
Leave before the heat makes travel difficult. Let your household contact know where you are and when you will check in.
guides.overview: A confirmed cool destination is the important output. A room that was tolerable an hour ago may no longer be suitable for a person with extra cooling or medical needs.

guides.title: Check a flooded home from outside first
guides.scenario: The road is open again, but that tells you little about the condition of the house.
steps: Wait for local authorities to permit return and approach only by a dry, open route.

From a safe location look for downed lines, sagging walls, displaced foundations, water at outlets or a gas odor. Move away and call the utility or emergency services if a hazard is present; make calls away from a possible gas leak.
Keep everyone outside if structural or electrical safety is uncertain. Arrange qualified inspection of flooded systems before power is restored.
Record who assessed the property and which areas, if any, are cleared. Give the same information to anyone arriving to help.
guides.overview: An all-clear for the neighborhood and a safe entry for a particular home are two separate decisions. Record the latter before organizing cleanup.
sources: National Weather Service · During a flood

illustrations.step: From a safe location look for downed lines, sagging walls, displaced foundations, water at outlets or a gas odor. Move away and call the utility or emergency services if a hazard is present; make calls away from a possible gas leak.
illustrations.title: Observe from outside
illustrations.alt: Observe from outside. Stay well away from damaged structures and lines. From a safe distance, note the address and what you can see.
illustrations.caption: Stay well away from damaged structures and lines. From a safe distance, note the address and what you can see.

guides.title: Sort pantry food after floodwater reaches a shelf
guides.scenario: The jars still look sealed and the waterline is below the top of some containers.
steps: Enter only after the area is cleared as safe. Keep children and pets out and photograph the affected shelves if it is safe to do so.
Set aside unaffected food from above the flood line in a clean location. If contact is uncertain, treat the package as exposed.
Discard exposed home-canned food, packages with screw or snap lids, cardboard, cloth and plastic-wrapped food. Do not open containers for a taste or smell check.
Follow public-health guidance for disposal. Use clean supplies for the next meal and clean your hands before touching unaffected food.
guides.overview: Closures and packaging can admit contamination that is invisible from outside. Keep a simple list of discarded food if your insurer requests it.

illustrations.step: Set aside unaffected food from above the flood line in a clean location. If contact is uncertain, treat the package as exposed.
illustrations.title: Mark the waterline
illustrations.alt: Mark the waterline. Food below the observed flood line may have been exposed. Keep unaffected packages separate while assessing damage.
illustrations.caption: Food below the observed flood line may have been exposed. Keep unaffected packages separate while assessing damage.

guides.title: Build a storm-damage photo record
guides.scenario: Three people are ready to clear a damaged room and belongings will soon lose their original positions.
steps: Start only in areas cleared for entry. Photograph the whole room from the doorway before moving things.
Work clockwise and take a wide view, a close view of damage and a model label if safe and accessible. Give each item a number in the notebook.
Record the item, room, approximate age and what you did with it. Ask the insurer about inspection and disposal before discarding when safe and practical.
Save copies away from the damaged property. Keep temporary repair receipts and add them to the same claim record.
guides.overview: The sequence connects each close-up to a recognizable room and item. It is much easier to explain a loss when the overview photos survive cleanup.

illustrations.step: Work clockwise and take a wide view, a close view of damage and a model label if safe and accessible. Give each item a number in the notebook.
illustrations.title: Pair the room view and detail
illustrations.alt: An appliance in a room is paired with a close photo of its model and serial label.
illustrations.caption: Give both images the same inventory number and record their location.

guides.title: Open a storm expense and call ledger
guides.scenario: A hotel receipt, a repair estimate and an insurer callback number are in three different places.
steps: Use the claims number on the insurance declarations page. Give the policy number if available, property address, date of damage and a reachable phone number. Ask for the claim number and adjuster’s contact. Write both at the top of the ledger. In Texas, if you cannot identify your insurer’s number, the state insurance help line is 800-252-3439 on weekdays.
Give each expense a line with date, vendor, amount, purpose and receipt location. Photograph paper receipts while still legible.
For a call, record the representative, time, promised action and date to follow up. Ask for material instructions in writing.
Keep paid amounts, estimates and reimbursements in separate columns. Check discrepancies against the actual policy with the insurer.
guides.overview: A running ledger distinguishes money spent from quotes and payments still pending. It gives either partner enough context to take the next call.
sources: Texas Department of Insurance · Help after a storm

illustrations.step: Give each expense a line with date, vendor, amount, purpose and receipt location. Photograph paper receipts while still legible.
illustrations.title: Give each expense its own row
illustrations.alt: A paper ledger pairs an expense with a receipt ID. The next expense starts on a fresh row.
illustrations.caption: Write the receipt identifier beside the amount. Use the same identifier in the image filename or paper envelope.

guides.title: Reset the kitchen after a water advisory ends
guides.scenario: The utility has lifted its notice, but yesterday’s ice is still in the freezer.
steps: Wait for the utility to lift the advisory for your address. Write down which taps to run, for how long, and what to do about filters and ice. If you missed the notice, call the supplier on your bill. Friendswood city water customers can call 281-996-3382. Keep using stored safe water until you have those directions.
Identify every affected outlet, dispenser, ice maker and filter. Keep stored safe water available while you work through the list.
Discard affected ice and follow the utility and appliance manufacturer’s directions for flushing, cleaning and any filter replacement. Avoid guessing a universal flushing time.
Mark each outlet complete. Remove reminder labels only once that outlet and its connected equipment are back in service.
guides.overview: Lifting an advisory restores the public supply. The outlet-by-outlet check addresses water or ice still held inside household equipment.
sources: City of Friendswood · Water and Wastewater Utilities

guides.title: Repack the kit after you actually use it
guides.scenario: The storm passes and a half-empty bag goes back into the closet.
steps: Lay the kit out in a dry place. Separate items used, damaged, expired and still ready.
Make a purchase or refill list with the exact battery, size or part name. Return borrowed cables and add replacements that stay packed.
Ask each person which item was hard to find and which was unnecessary. Change one pocket or label and have the other person locate it.
Mark the refill as pending until the replacement is physically in the bag. Date the next check and return the kit to its agreed location.
guides.overview: A kit is ready again when its missing items have been replaced and both people can find them. The most valuable change may be moving one item to the outside pocket.

guides.title: Rehearse the plan in twenty minutes
guides.scenario: Choose an ordinary evening. Imagine that one of you is away when a water outage and a street closure happen together.
steps: Give each person a starting location. Without coaching, ask each to find the water reserve, identify the official information source and name the meeting point.
Introduce one complication, such as a dead phone or a pet at home. Have each person describe the next action and who needs to hear about it.
Compare answers. Write down the first point at which the two plans diverged, then fix that card, phone number or storage location.
Repeat just the failed portion and date the revision. Leave alarms, utilities and essential equipment operating throughout the practice.
guides.overview: The drill is finished when both people can make the same next decision using the information they will actually have. Keep the revised card wherever the practice revealed a gap.

guides.title: Shelter during a tornado warning
guides.scenario: A tornado warning lights up the phone while you are upstairs. Your planned hurricane destination is across town.
steps: Go immediately to the safe room or storm shelter. In a sturdy building without one, move to a small windowless interior room on the lowest safe level.
Bring anyone beside you, crouch low and protect heads and necks with your arms or something already within reach. Stay away from windows.
Listen to official alerts and stay sheltered until the warning passes. If you live in a mobile home, arrange a sturdy shelter and move there ahead of severe weather when possible.
guides.overview: Choose the room on a calm day and practice getting there from the bedroom. When a warning arrives, you should already know which door to open.

guides.title: Stop outdoor work when thunder starts
guides.scenario: Rain has yet to reach the greenhouse, but you hear thunder while putting away tools.
steps: Leave the garden, pool, open shelter or greenhouse immediately. Go inside a substantial building with wiring or plumbing, or an enclosed metal-topped vehicle with the windows up.
Inside, stay away from windows, plumbing and equipment connected to wiring. Postpone showers and outdoor checks.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out. Each new rumble restarts the wait.
guides.overview: The sound of thunder is enough to change the plan. Name a reachable shelter before beginning work so you never need to finish a task outdoors to earn the break.

guides.title: Decide who can enter a damp home after a flood
guides.scenario: A room has stayed wet for two days and a family member with asthma wants to help move furniture.
steps: Wait for structural and electrical clearance. If the building stayed wet beyond 24–48 hours, assume mold may be present even where you cannot see it.
Keep people with asthma or other lung disease, compromised immunity, and children away from moldy areas and cleanup. Arrange an alternative place to stay if needed.
From a safe location record the water source, time wet and affected rooms. Call the insurer and qualified remediation help for extensive damage or sewage contamination.
Before reoccupying, confirm the moisture source is repaired, damaged material is addressed and the area is clean and dry.
guides.overview: Dry paint on the surface is a poor test of what is behind a wall. The return decision involves both the state of the building and the health of the people who would enter.
sources: CDC · Mold exposure after severe weather

guides.title: Set up a cleaner-air room during wildfire smoke
guides.scenario: Smoke has traveled into Friendswood overnight. The house is safe to occupy, but the outdoor air is unhealthy and both of you need a place to sleep.
gear: Portable particle air cleaner sized for the room
guides.time: Before smoke arrives or when advised
steps: Follow local evacuation instructions first. If sheltering during smoke, choose a room that stays cool, has few outside openings and fits everyone. When available, enter your location on the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map and check fine-particle conditions nearby. During an internet outage, use local radio advisories and start reducing exposure if smoke is present.
Close exterior doors and windows. Where the cooling system has a fresh-air intake setting, select recirculation according to its instructions. Keep exits clear.
Place a room-sized air cleaner that does not produce ozone where its vents are clear. Run it continuously at the highest tolerable speed. Avoid frying, burning candles and smoking indoors.
Check on heat, smoke and anyone feeling unwell. If power fails, the room gets too hot or smoke keeps entering, move to a cleaner, cooler building. When outdoor air improves, ventilate the room.
guides.overview: Choose your backup address while the air is clear. In a Gulf Coast summer, a closed bedroom can become too hot to use long before the smoke outdoors clears.
sources: EPA · Create a clean room during a wildfire
AirNow · Using the Fire and Smoke Map

guides.title: Rehearse seven days without power in Friendswood
guides.scenario: On paper, it is August. The power went out at breakfast, the utility has no firm restoration time, and a friend across town has offered a cool room. What would make the two of you leave today?
steps: Leave the electricity, cooling, medicine storage and medical equipment running throughout this tabletop exercise. On one page draw seven day columns and make rows for drinking water, meals, cooling, medicine or powered equipment, and contact with someone outside the house.

Hour one. One person records the outage start, checks alerts and finds the refrigerator outage guide. The other identifies any immediate dependency on power and calls the proposed host in this rehearsal only if you have arranged it. Write down a reachable destination, a ride and a second option.

First night. Build a meal for two from food already safe at room temperature. Count the water the meal and both people would use. Enter it in the log. Use your pharmacist’s or equipment provider’s actual storage limits and backup instructions. Mark anything unknown for follow-up.

Day three. Imagine the first host loses power too. Swap roles. Using yesterday’s water use and what remains, work out when you must resupply. Pick a departure time that leaves enough daylight and cooling, water and device power for the trip. Move it earlier if any essential need cannot be met.

Days four to seven. Fill the remaining columns at the location you chose. Name who confirms drinking water, needed equipment, a place to sleep and the next check-in. If either of you assumes a delivery or a ride, identify the person who can confirm it and an alternative if it falls through.

Compare the two decisions you made: when to leave and when it is safe to return. Circle the first unconfirmed dependency, give one person the job of resolving it and write the answer on the household card.
guides.overview: The most revealing entry is often the first blank square. Seven days of pantry food can coexist with one afternoon of usable battery power. The earlier limit sets your timetable.
